messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Editor
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Violence: Violence, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me, Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 74, Graham had the careful, restrained manner of someone who had spent a long time making himself small in order to stay safe. He was an American man of Oceania background, divorced, and had worked for many years as an editor, a role that had once suited his precision and tolerance for close reading. He came to treatment after months of feeling increasingly unsettled by ordinary exchanges that other people seemed to experience as harmless. The most reliable spark was criticism. If a colleague at the publishing office pointed out a sentence that needed changing, or if a younger editor corrected a detail in a manuscript, Graham would feel his chest tighten and his mind go blank with the same old sense that he was being put in his place. Violence in films, even brief scenes of pushing or shouting, could leave him unable to concentrate for the rest of the day. He also found himself reacting strongly when he saw the man who had hurt him, a person he had tried hard to avoid but who remained part of the same small social world, making accidental sightings painfully possible.

The trauma he described had happened years earlier, during a relationship that had begun as companionable and gradually become controlling. His former partner had criticized the way Graham spoke, dressed, and organized the household, and those corrections had increasingly sharpened into intimidation. The worst episode came one evening after an argument over something trivial, when the partner struck him and then shoved him against the wall of their apartment. Graham recalled that night not as a smooth story but as a handful of frozen images. In his account, each moment arrived like a separate picture: the lamp tilted on the side table, the man’s hand raised, the feel of the wall at his back, the look on the offender’s face. He said that when he tried to think about it, it did not feel like a memory of his own life so much as something he had witnessed happening to someone else. Yet the old rage came back with it, sudden and intense, making his jaw clench and his hands tremble. He had never been able to make sense of why it happened to him, except to settle on a painful explanation that there must have been something about who he was that made him an acceptable target. Over time, he came to think of himself as less than fully human, more like an object that could be handled, corrected, or damaged. He also feared that he would never feel normal emotions again, as though some vital part of him had been knocked flat and could not be restored.

After the relationship ended, Graham tried to carry on with his life through routines that kept strong feeling at bay. He threw himself into work tasks that required attention to detail and spent long stretches of time distracting himself with reading, proofreading, or television. When anything reminded him of the man who had harmed him—a familiar street, a voice with the same inflection, a glimpse of someone with a similar build—he would steer away or leave the area altogether. At home he organized his days to avoid stillness, because quiet moments made room for the pictures to surface. He was careful not to let himself feel much of anything, not even anger or sadness, because he was afraid that if he opened the door to one strong emotion, the whole store of what he had been holding back would rush in. This pattern had narrowed his life in practical ways. He had become more guarded at work, less willing to engage in the lively back-and-forth of editing meetings, and more prone to stepping out when conversations turned sharp. He noticed that he was often absent in spirit even when present in the room, as if some part of him were standing at a distance from his own life.

By the time he sought help, what distressed him most was how readily the present could collapse into the past. A simple correction in the office, a scene of aggression on television, or the sudden appearance of the former partner in town could leave him shaken, angry, and detached in the same breath. He came to treatment not because he believed he could easily forget what happened, but because he was frightened by how much of his life had come to be organized around avoiding it. He hoped for some way to sit with criticism, violence on the page or screen, and the possibility of seeing that man again without feeling reduced to that wall, those few dreadful moments, and the object-like version of himself that had stayed with him ever since.
